updates.expected: FermatMind uses the six RIASEC interest areas. Explore how the 60-question and 140-question versions calculate scores, how your three-letter Holland Code is formed and how to use it for career exploration.
updates.value: Holland’s vocational interest theory focuses on the relationship between people and work environments. It organizes activity interests into six areas: Realistic (R), Investigative (I), Artistic (A), Social (S), Enterprising (E), and Conventional (C). Most people combine several areas, and work environments can likewise be understood through their characteristic tasks and activity demands. FermatMind uses a self-report questionnaire to build your six-interest profile, summarize the three relatively strongest areas, and preserve the full distribution and score gaps so you can compare courses, work tasks, and career-exploration options. Interests describe what you are more willing to engage in; they do not establish ability. Career decisions should also consider skills, values, practical constraints, and direct experience.

updates.expected:
Holland’s RIASEC model describes six work-activity interests: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional. It concerns activities you tend to enjoy, not abilities you have already demonstrated.

Enjoying analysis does not mean you have research skills, and enjoying organization does not guarantee management suitability. Connect your combination of interests to real tasks rather than remembering only a letter label.
updates.value:
Holland’s vocational interest theory, developed by psychologist John Holland, explains career exploration through the relationship between personal interests and work environments. RIASEC organizes activity interests into six areas: Realistic (R), working with tools, equipment, and tangible things; Investigative (I), analyzing problems and exploring how things work; Artistic (A), creating and expressing ideas independently; Social (S), helping, teaching, and supporting others; Enterprising (E), persuading, organizing, and advancing goals; and Conventional (C), organizing information, following procedures, and maintaining order.

The six areas form a hexagonal model in the R–I–A–S–E–C order to summarize similarities among interests: adjacent types usually share more characteristics, while types farther apart are generally less alike. This is a model for understanding interest structure. It does not require your scores to form a regular shape, and it does not mean you belong to only one type. Most people combine several interests, and the same occupation can involve multiple kinds of activities.

FermatMind shows the full six-interest profile first, then uses the top three areas to summarize relatively prominent directions. When scores are close, compare your engagement and willingness to persist in specific tasks instead of overinterpreting small changes in letter order. Use the results to plan course trials, projects, or career conversations, then weigh skills, values, and working conditions. An interest assessment provides exploration clues; it does not establish occupational ability or guarantee job fit or career success.
